stem: Recording a building at the price paid for it many years ago is an example of …

options.content: historic cost
options.rationale: Correct: assets are kept at their original cost.

options.content: net realisable value
options.rationale: This is the expected selling price less costs, used for inventory.

options.content: the going concern concept
options.rationale: Going concern assumes the business will continue; it is not about the purchase price.

options.content: the realisation concept
options.rationale: Realisation is about when revenue is recognised.

explanation: Historic cost is objective but may be out of date.

stem: Which of the following is a **non-financial** factor that the statements do not show?

options.content: The skills and experience of the workforce
options.rationale: Correct: these cannot be measured reliably in money.

options.content: The wages paid during the year
options.rationale: Wages are an expense in the income statement.

options.content: The value of inventory at the year end
options.rationale: Inventory appears in the statement of financial position.

options.content: The amount owed by credit customers
options.rationale: Trade receivables are a current asset.

explanation: Money measurement means only items with a money value are recorded; staff skills are left out.

stem: A business owns land bought in 2005, shown at cost. Its current value is much higher. What effect does historic cost have on ROCE?

options.content: ROCE is understated because capital employed is too high
options.rationale: Undervalued assets make capital employed too low, not too high.

options.content: ROCE is overstated because profit is too low
options.rationale: A lower profit would reduce ROCE.

options.content: ROCE is unaffected because land is not depreciated
options.rationale: Land is still part of capital employed.

options.content: ROCE is overstated because capital employed is too low
options.rationale: Correct: the same profit is divided by an undervalued capital employed.

explanation: Assets at old costs understate capital employed, so ROCE looks better than the return on current values.
hints: ROCE = profit before interest ÷ capital employed.

stem: Two businesses make identical sales and purchases, but one estimates a shorter useful life for its vehicles. Compared with the other, its statements will show …

options.content: higher profit and higher vehicle net book value
options.rationale: This is the effect of a longer life.

options.content: lower gross profit
options.rationale: Depreciation is below gross profit.

options.content: lower profit and lower vehicle net book value
options.rationale: Correct: a shorter life means a larger annual depreciation charge.

options.content: no difference, because cash spent is the same
options.rationale: Profit depends on the depreciation estimate, not the cash spent.

explanation: Estimates such as useful life change profit and asset values from the same transactions.

stem: Which accounting concept explains why a business's good reputation is not shown in its statements?

options.content: Duality
options.rationale: Duality is about the two-sided effect of transactions.

options.content: Consistency
options.rationale: Consistency is about using the same methods each year.

options.content: Money measurement
options.rationale: Correct: only items that can be measured reliably in money are recorded.

options.content: Matching
options.rationale: Matching relates expenses to the income of the period.

explanation: Reputation cannot be measured reliably in money, so it is left out.

stem: An investor is studying a Harare taxi company's latest statements. Which piece of information would the statements **not** reveal?

options.content: The cost of fuel used in the year
options.rationale: Fuel is an expense in the income statement.

options.content: Fuel prices will rise next year
options.rationale: Correct: future economic conditions are not in historical statements.

options.content: The net book value of the vehicles
options.rationale: This is in the statement of financial position.

options.content: The loan outstanding at the year end
options.rationale: Loans are liabilities in the statement of financial position.

explanation: Statements are historical; expected changes in the economic climate are not recorded.
hints: Statements record what has already happened.

stem: Why do accountants use historic cost despite its limitations?

options.content: It always shows the current value of assets
options.rationale: It does not; that is its main limitation.

options.content: It gives the highest possible profit
options.rationale: Historic cost is used for reliability, not to raise profit.

options.content: It is required only for service businesses
options.rationale: Historic cost applies to all businesses.

options.content: It is objective and can be checked against invoices
options.rationale: Correct: the original price is a fact, not an opinion.

explanation: Historic cost is reliable and verifiable, even if it becomes out of date.

stem: A bank is deciding whether to lend to a small poultry farm. Which non-financial factor is likely to matter most alongside the farm's ratios?

options.content: The farm's profit margin last year
options.rationale: This is a financial figure already available from the statements.

options.content: The owner's experience and the reliability of feed supplies
options.rationale: Correct: these affect the farm's future ability to repay but are not in the statements.

options.content: The farm's current ratio
options.rationale: This is a financial ratio.

options.content: The depreciation method used for the fowl runs
options.rationale: This is an accounting policy, shown in the notes, not a non-financial factor.

explanation: Skills, supply chains, disease risk and the economic climate all affect repayment but are outside the statements.
hints: Non-financial factors cannot be found in the statements.

stem: Financial statements show the value of a business's skilled workforce as an asset.
explanation: False. Staff skills cannot be measured reliably in money, so they are not recorded.

stem: Two businesses with identical transactions can report different profits because they choose different depreciation methods.
explanation: True. Accounting policies and estimates change reported profit.

stem: Match each situation with the limitation of accounting statements it illustrates.

left.content: Premises bought in 2010 are shown at their 2010 price
One shop allows 2% for irrecoverable debts, another 6%
A key manager is about to leave
Machinery is depreciated over 4 years by one firm and 8 years by another
A new road will take customers away from the shop

explanation: Old prices are a historic cost issue; allowances and useful lives are estimates; staff and location changes are non-financial.

payload.template: Financial statements are {{blank:a}}: they record past transactions in money, at the {{blank:b}} cost of assets, using {{blank:c}} chosen by the business.

explanation: These are the main limitations examined.

stem: A business has capital employed of US\$144,000, which includes land at its cost of US\$30,000. The land is now worth US\$96,000. Profit before interest was US\$21,600. Calculate the ROCE if the land were shown at its current value, to one decimal place.
explanation: Capital employed at current value = 144,000 − 30,000 + 96,000 = 210,000. ROCE = 21,600 ÷ 210,000 × 100 = 10.3% (compared with 15.0% at historic cost). Adding the value without removing the cost gives 9.0%.
workedSolution: 1. Capital employed at current value = 144,000 − 30,000 + 96,000 = 210,000. ROCE = 21,600 ÷ 210,000 × 100 = 10.3% (compared with 15.0% at historic cost). Adding the value without removing the cost gives 9.0%.
hints: Replace the land's cost with its current value in capital employed.

stem: Two firms each buy machinery for US\$48,000 with no residual value and use straight-line depreciation. Firm A estimates a useful life of 4 years; Firm B estimates 8 years. By how much is Firm A's annual profit lower than Firm B's, all else being equal?

In their first year, two shops each have trade receivables of US\$26,400. One makes an allowance for irrecoverable debts of 2%, the other 5%. What is the difference between their profits caused by this estimate?
Explain **one** limitation of using historic cost in the statement of financial position.

points.description: Assets bought long ago are shown at old prices / below current value
So the statement understates the business's worth (or overstates ROCE / makes comparisons misleading)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Premises bought years ago are still shown at their original price, which may be far below their value today, so the statement understates the resources of the business and makes its ROCE look higher than it really is.

explanation: Name it and explain its effect.

stem: Thandeka plans to buy a grocery shop in Bulawayo. Its statements show strong ratios. Suggest **three** non-financial factors she should investigate before buying.

points.description: Workforce: skills, experience, whether key staff will stay
Location: customer numbers, competition nearby, lease terms, security
Economic climate / reputation / supplier relationships / condition of premises

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She should find out whether the experienced staff will stay after the sale, whether a new supermarket is planned nearby or the lease is about to end, and how changes in prices and customers' incomes could affect sales.

explanation: Non-financial factors affect future success but are not in the statements.
hints: People, place and the wider economy.

stem: Mutare Hardware Ltd's statement of financial position at 31 December 2025 shows capital employed of US\$175,000. This includes premises bought in 2009 at a cost of US\$40,000; an estate agent values them at US\$120,000 today. Profit for the year was US\$26,250; the company has no loans. Its machinery is depreciated over 10 years, whereas most similar businesses use 6 years. Its most experienced manager retires next month.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the ROCE based on the statement of financial position, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the ROCE if the premises were shown at their current value, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: If the company used a 6-year life for its machinery like similar businesses, its profit for the year would be …

options.content: higher
options.rationale: A shorter life increases depreciation and reduces profit.

options.content: lower
options.rationale: Correct: a shorter life means a bigger annual depreciation charge.

options.content: unchanged
options.rationale: Depreciation is an expense, so profit would change.

options.content: unchanged, but gross profit would fall
options.rationale: Depreciation is below gross profit.

parts.explanation: A shorter useful life raises the depreciation charge.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Using the information, explain **two** limitations of relying on the company's statements to judge its performance.

points.description: Historic cost: premises at 2009 cost understate capital employed
So ROCE of 15.0% overstates the true return (10.3% on current values)
Accounting policy/estimate: 10-year machinery life is longer than usual, so depreciation is low and profit flattered / not comparable with similar businesses
Non-financial: the experienced manager's retirement is not shown but may hurt future results

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: First, historic cost: the premises are shown at their 2009 price, so capital employed is understated and the ROCE of 15.0% looks better than the 10.3% earned on current values. Second, the company's depreciation estimate is generous: a 10-year life gives a lower charge than the 6 years used by similar firms, so its profit is flattered and cannot be compared directly. (Also, the statements say nothing about the experienced manager retiring.)

parts.explanation: Two limitations, each named and linked to the case (2 marks each).

explanation: ROCE 15.0% at historic cost; 10.3% on current values.
hints: Replace the premises' cost with their current value in capital employed.

stem:
Two new courier businesses in Harare each had revenue of US\$124,000, gross profit of US\$37,200, other expenses of US\$18,600, a van costing US\$24,000 (no residual value, straight-line depreciation) and trade receivables of US\$15,000 at the end of their first year.

| Estimate | Courier A | Courier B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Useful life of van | 4 years | 6 years |
| Allowance for irrecoverable debts | 4% | 1% |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate Courier A's profit for the year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate Courier B's profit for the year.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate Courier B's profit margin, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the difference in profit does not show that Courier B is better managed.

points.description: Both businesses had identical trading results
The difference comes only from estimates (useful life, allowance) chosen by each owner

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Their revenue, gross profit and expenses were the same. Courier B reports US\$2,450 more profit only because it estimates a longer van life and a smaller allowance for irrecoverable debts.

hints: Depreciation = cost ÷ useful life; allowance = % × receivables.
